nodes.label: Music as culture
nodes.one_line: Explain a tradition's music with Merriam's tripartite model — conceptualization, behavior, sound — and show how a single performance instantiates all three layers.
know_what: Merriam's tripartite model — conceptualization, behavior, sound, the three layers of The Anthropology of Music (1964) that moved the field from studying sound to studying music as human behavior
conceptualization — what the culture believes music is and does: the ideas, values, and categories held before any sound is made
behavior — the actions that produce and surround sound: who may perform, when, where, for whom, and what they do while playing
sound — the audible product, the only layer pre-Merriam music study habitually examined
'music in culture' vs 'music as culture' — Merriam's formula (music embedded in culture) against the later claim (e.g., Feld's) that music is not merely carried by culture but constitutes it
the performance as the unit — one event instantiating all three layers at once, the field's preferred analytic starting point
Blacking's Venda material — How Musical Is Man (1973), where children's songs show that music's meaning lives in the social relations that produce it, not in the notes
Nettl's formulation — The Study of Ethnomusicology (1983, 2005) reading music as a system of behavior and belief first, sound second
know_how: Split any performance you witness into the three layers: what people think about the music, what they do around it, what sounds result
Explain one performance with all three layers, showing a causal chain — a belief at the conceptualization layer shaping a behavior that shapes the sound
Diagnose an account that is sound-only and add the missing behavior and conceptualization layers to it
Ask the cultural questions at each layer: who is excluded from performing, when is this music appropriate, what counts as playing well
Check your three-layer account against practitioners' own categories before finalizing, so the layers are theirs, not imported
Use the model comparatively: run the same three questions against two performances and note which layer differs most
habits: Never describe a sound without asking what behavior produced it and what belief shapes that behavior
Ask of every performance who is excluded, and treat the answer as data
Run the tripartite split as a checklist on every field observation, not as a theory to recite
When reading an old comparative study, notice which of the three layers it silently dropped
Ask what the music does in the culture before asking what it is
nodes.checkpoint: Take a single performance you have witnessed or recorded and produce a one-page account organized as Merriam's three layers — conceptualization, behavior, sound — with at least two specific observations per layer and a sentence showing how a belief at one layer shaped what happened at another.
nodes.common_failure: Reducing the model to a slogan — 'music is culture!' — and then describing only the sound layer anyway: the tripartite claim appears in the introduction, but the analysis stays note-level, with no account of who may perform, when, and why.
sources: Alan P. Merriam, The Anthropology of Music (1964)
John Blacking, How Musical Is Man (1973)
Bruno Nettl, The Study of Ethnomusicology (2005)

nodes.label: Defining music across cultures
nodes.one_line: Argue where the category 'music' begins and ends for a given community using Blacking's 'humanly organized sound' and Nettl's cross-cultural definitions, instead of assuming your own boundary.
know_what: 'humanly organized sound' — Blacking's working definition in How Musical Is Man (1973): sound organized by people, whatever its local function
the cross-cultural survey of definitions — Nettl's finding that many cultures have no word equivalent to 'music', classifying sound by function, ritual, or emotion instead
the functional boundary — where a community draws the line between music and noise, music and ritual sound, music and speech
song vs speech — cultures that separate the two differently than the West does (chant, recitation, drummed speech sitting on the boundary)
the category problem — applying 'music' to traditions whose sound practices are organized as prayer, healing, or communication
emic vs etic definitions — insider categories vs analyst-imposed ones, the test for whether a boundary is the community's or yours
musical universals — the search for features common to all musics, and the critics who say the search itself imports the category
know_how: Ask the community's own boundary questions before defining anything: what do you call this sound, who makes it, when is it appropriate, what is it for
Test Blacking's definition against a case: does the community's practice count as 'humanly organized sound', and what does that framing add or hide
Locate where a tradition's classification of sound diverges from the Western 'music' category and state the divergence precisely
Run the emic/etic test on your own working definition and say whose category it is
State your operational definition before comparing two traditions, so the boundary is explicit and checkable
When a translation ('song', 'dance', 'ritual') carries a Western category into another language, flag it rather than absorbing it
habits: Ask what the practitioners call this before asking what this is
Check whether the language even has a word for 'music' and what territory it covers
Treat your own definition of music as a choice to be defended, not a given
Notice when a word you habitually use ('piece', 'concert', 'genre') smuggles in a Western boundary
Before any comparative claim, re-state the definition you are comparing under

know_why.claim: 'Music' names a universal human category: Blacking's 'humanly organized sound' and Nettl's cross-cultural survey show that every society organizes sound meaningfully, so the analyst may study any tradition with the same conceptual toolbox.
know_why.because: If the category were not universal, comparison would be impossible — a shared, maximally inclusive definition is what lets ethnomusicology treat a Venda children's song and a Javanese gamelan piece as the same kind of object at all.
know_why.disputed_by: the constructivist camp — ethnographers and critical musicologists such as Steven Feld (the Kaluli organize sound as bird song, weeping, and water, not 'music') and Gary Tomlinson, who hold that the label 'music' is a Western construct that misdescribes traditions whose sound practices are organized as ritual, healing, or speech.
know_why.source: John Blacking, How Musical Is Man (1973); Bruno Nettl, The Study of Ethnomusicology (2005), ch. 1-2; Steven Feld, Sound and Sentiment (1982); Gary Tomlinson, A Million Years of Music (2015)

nodes.checkpoint: Take one tradition you have studied and write a half-page argument for where its 'music' category begins and ends — using Blacking's definition, Nettl's cross-cultural findings, and the community's own terms — and state explicitly what your boundary includes and excludes.
nodes.common_failure: Assuming the Western boundary: treating 'music' as self-evident and classifying a tradition's sound practices by your own genres, so a healing song or ritual drumming gets filed under 'music' in a sense the practitioners do not share — the exact imposition the constructivist critique attacks.
sources: John Blacking, How Musical Is Man (1973)
Bruno Nettl, The Study of Ethnomusicology (2005)
Steven Feld, Sound and Sentiment (1982)

nodes.label: Bi-musicality
nodes.one_line: Learn to perform a short piece in the tradition you study well enough to play it for a practitioner, following Mantle Hood's bi-musicality program.
know_what: bi-musicality — Mantle Hood's term ('The Challenge of Bi-Musicality', 1960): learning to perform the tradition you study as a condition of understanding it
the UCLA program — Hood's Institute of Ethnomusicology, where 1960s students learned Indonesian gamelan and other ensembles as coursework, performing alongside analysis
Hood's claim — insight into a music comes through performance, not only through listening, transcription, and theory
the performance threshold — a short piece played well enough for a practitioner to recognize it, Hood's own formulation of the goal
performance knowledge — the bodily, tacit competence (feel, timing, social choreography) that notation and analysis cannot carry
the apprenticeship contrast — traditions whose own pedagogy is lifelong and embodied (Indian guru-śiṣya paramparā, Javanese court musicianship), which the semester model compresses
the insider/outsider debate — whether the researcher's performance is genuine musicianship or a gesture, the standing charge against the program
Rice's model — Timothy Rice's May It Fill Your Soul (1994), built on his own performance study of Bulgarian music, the program's most cited vindication
know_how: Find a teacher or a high-quality video of a practitioner and learn one short piece phrase by phrase, imitating exactly before varying anything
Learn by ear and imitation first, notation later — most traditions teach orally, and the ear route preserves what notation drops
Practice against the recording at performance tempo, matching timing and ornamentation, not just the pitches
Perform the piece from memory for a practitioner and get their judgment: recognizable, correct, acceptable — the three-part test
Log practice sessions with the specific technique each one targeted, so the 40 hours are accountable
Use the performance as an analytical instrument: after each session, note in the field journal what the body now knows that listening never revealed
habits: Imitate first, understand later — play the phrase exactly before asking what it means
Ask your teacher what you are doing wrong, and fix that before adding anything new
Never simplify the ornamentation to make the piece easier; the ornamentation is the tradition
Record your own practice and compare it against the model phrase by phrase
Treat every performance session as data collection, with field notes the same evening

know_why.claim: Learning to perform the tradition is a necessary route to understanding it: Hood's bi-musicality program holds that insight comes through doing, and the researcher must acquire the musicianship, not only analyze recordings.
know_why.because: A tradition's essential knowledge — feel, timing, the social choreography of performance — lives in the body and is invisible to transcription and listening, so the analyst who has never performed will miss precisely what practitioners know.
know_why.disputed_by: critics who call the program tokenism — postcolonial and insider critics such as Kofi Agawu, who argue that no outsider genuinely acquires the tradition's musicianship in a short program, and that the bi-musical gesture lets the researcher claim an authority the performance does not confer.
know_why.source: Mantle Hood, 'The Challenge of Bi-Musicality' (1960); Timothy Rice, May It Fill Your Soul (1994); Kofi Agawu, Representing African Music (2003)

nodes.checkpoint: Learn one short piece in the tradition you study and perform it from memory at performance tempo, with the tradition's ornamentation, for a practitioner who confirms it is recognizable and acceptable.
nodes.common_failure: Learning a simplified approximation — the notes without the feel — and calling it bi-musicality: the piece is recognizable to you but not to the tradition's musicians, so the exercise produces neither musicianship nor insight, only the gesture the critics warn about.
sources: Mantle Hood, 'The Challenge of Bi-Musicality' (1960)
Timothy Rice, May It Fill Your Soul (1994)
Kofi Agawu, Representing African Music (2003)

nodes.label: RILM literature search
nodes.one_line: Search RILM Abstracts of Music Literature by topic, region, and instrument to find the peer-reviewed scholarship on any tradition in under an hour.
know_what: RILM Abstracts of Music Literature — the annotated international bibliography of music scholarship since 1967, covering articles, books, and dissertations
the RILM abstract — each entry carries an author-written English abstract, letting you screen relevance without the full text
RILM's controlled vocabulary — the indexing terms for instruments, regions, genres, and peoples that make a topic searchable beyond free-text keywords
the geographic and chronological indexes — RILM's routes for bounding a tradition's literature by place and period
the scholarly filter — RILM indexes peer-reviewed and vetted literature, not blogs or program notes
related databases — JSTOR's music titles, Ethnomusicology: Global Field Recordings, the MLA International Bibliography, and how their coverage differs from RILM's
forward citation — following who has cited a foundational study (via RILM's cited-reference links or Google Scholar) to track a debate after its origin
know_how: Run a topic search with region and instrument as facets — e.g., 'gamelan' + 'Java' + 'tuning' — and screen the hits by abstract, inside an hour
Search the controlled vocabulary, not free text alone: try RILM's thesaurus terms for the instrument and the people before resorting to keywords
Use the geographic and chronological indexes to bound the literature on a tradition, then scan the bounded set for the core studies
Harvest the foundational citations from a recent ethnography's bibliography and check each in RILM for abstracts and forward citations
Record the search — database, date, query, and result count — so the search is reproducible and citable
When a tradition is under-covered in RILM, name the gap and turn to area bibliographies: the journal Ethnomusicology's book notes, regional journals, and archive catalogs
habits: Search the literature before designing the study, so your questions are not already answered
Re-run the search six months later — the literature moves
Keep the search log with the project files, not in memory
When a search returns nothing, doubt the query before the field
Record the search date on every bibliography, because a search is a snapshot
nodes.checkpoint: Given a tradition, instrument, or region, run a RILM search and produce an annotated list of the 5-10 peer-reviewed sources most relevant to your question — abstracts screened, citations recorded, search logged with database, date, and query — in under an hour.
nodes.common_failure: Treating the search as a Google query: free-text keywords that miss RILM's controlled vocabulary and geographic indexes, so the results skip the core ethnomusicological literature and the project later re-invents a question the field already answered.
sources: RILM Abstracts of Music Literature, database help and thesaurus (rilm.org)
Jennifer C. Post, Ethnomusicology: A Research and Information Guide (2nd ed., 2011)

nodes.label: Research questions
nodes.one_line: Turn a curiosity about a music culture into three answerable research questions — descriptive, comparative, or applied — each with the observable evidence it implies.
know_what: the research question — the single answerable question a study is organized around; every design decision follows from it
descriptive questions — what the music is, who does it, when and where: the documentary and ethnographic baseline
comparative questions — how this tradition compares to another, or to another period, on a defined dimension
applied questions — what research can do for the community: revitalization, documentation, repatriation support
the answerability test — a question is researchable when you can name the observable evidence that would answer it
the one-line purpose — the distilled question that the fieldwork plan, interview guide, and analysis all answer to
the literature gap — the space the question occupies that existing scholarship has not filled, found via the RILM search
hypothesis vs question — the scientific school's preference for testable hypotheses against the interpretive school's open questions, a choice the researcher must make, not inherit
know_how: Turn one curiosity into three questions, one of each type — descriptive, comparative, applied — and pick the one that fits your access and skills
Apply the answerability test to each: name the evidence that would answer it, and cut any question whose evidence you cannot reach
Write the question as one sentence with a verb and an object — 'How do X musicians negotiate Y in Z?' — never 'What is X music like?'
Ground the question in the literature gap, citing the sources from your RILM search that leave it open
Scope the question to the access you actually have: a question needing year-round ritual access is not researchable in a two-week visit
Draft the one-line purpose that the fieldwork plan, interview guide, and analysis will each answer to
habits: Ask 'what would answer this?' before 'is this interesting?'
Rewrite the question until a stranger can state the evidence it implies
When a question grows, split it; when it shrinks, drop it
Keep the gap visible: the question exists because the literature has not answered it
Test the question against the field site before leaving home
nodes.checkpoint: Produce three research questions — one descriptive, one comparative, one applied — each in a single sentence naming its evidence and the literature gap it fills, cited from your RILM search, so a supervisor can pick any of the three and plan fieldwork for it.
nodes.common_failure: Falling in love with a topic instead of a question: 'I want to study gamelan' never becomes answerable, so the study collects everything and argues nothing — the design has no spine and the analysis no claims.
sources: Bruno Nettl, The Study of Ethnomusicology (2005), 'The Nature of Research' chapters
Barz & Cooley, Shadows in the Field (2nd ed., 2008), ch. on fieldwork questions
John W. Creswell, Research Design (qualitative question design chapters)

nodes.label: Disciplinary debates
nodes.one_line: Articulate the emic/etic and scientific/interpretive debates and defend your own position with named practitioners on each side, instead of writing as if the field had one method.
know_what: the emic/etic distinction — Pike's terms borrowed from linguistics: emic = insider categories, etic = analyst categories; the field's longest-running methodological debate
the scientific program — the heir of 1880s comparative musicology (Stumpf, Hornbostel): measurement, systematic transcription, cantometrics-style coding, hypothesis testing
the interpretive program — the heir of Merriam (1964) and Geertz: music in culture, emic meaning, thick description
'music in culture' vs 'music as culture' — Merriam's embedding formula against the claim that music constitutes culture rather than sitting inside it
the insider/outsider debate — who may represent a tradition, sharpened by the postcolonial critique of Western scholars speaking for others
the applied turn — the 1990s-2000s demand that research return value to communities through collaboration and repatriation

named camps — each position has canonical practitioners: scientific (Stumpf, Hornbostel, Lomax), interpretive (Merriam, Feld, Rice), critical (Agawu), applied (the repatriation and collaboration literature)
the schools' trade-offs — each school optimises for something and gives something up, and a position paper must own both sides of that ledger
know_how: State the emic/etic distinction with an example from your own research: one claim in insider terms and one in analyst terms, labeled
Reconstruct any disciplinary debate as two positions, each with named practitioners and the evidence each side would accept — never an averaged middle
Defend your own position: name which school's questions your project answers and what choosing it gives up
Label every category you use as the tradition's (emic) or yours (etic), so the reader always knows whose concept is in play
Trace a current article's method back to the school that produced it, citing what that school optimizes for
Write the cost of your school's choice into the paper — per the schools' 'gives up' columns — instead of writing as if the field had one method
habits: When reading a study, ask which school's assumptions produced it before judging its findings
Before writing, state your own position and its cost in one sentence
When two camps disagree, report both positions before arguing yours
Never write 'ethnomusicologists believe X' — name the camp
Treat a consensus as the thing to interrogate: whose questions did it answer, and whose did it drop
nodes.checkpoint: Write a two-page position paper on one disciplinary debate (emic/etic or scientific/interpretive) that names at least two practitioners on each side, states the evidence each side accepts, and defends your own position with its acknowledged cost — readable by a colleague who takes the other side.
nodes.common_failure: Writing as if the field had settled on one method: presenting the interpretive consensus as 'the' way to study music, or averaging the camps into 'both matter' — which satisfies nobody and commits the paper to no position at all.
sources: Alan P. Merriam, The Anthropology of Music (1964)
Bruno Nettl, The Study of Ethnomusicology (2005), 'The Nature of the Field' chapters
Kofi Agawu, Representing African Music (2003)
Mark Slobin, 'Micromusics of the West' (1993), for the applied turn's questions

nodes.label: Access & entry
nodes.one_line: Identify the gatekeepers and introduction chains that grant access to a music community, and secure an explicit invitation before recording anything.
know_what: gatekeepers — the elders, ritual leaders, festival organizers, and officials whose permission unlocks access to a music community
the introduction chain — the social route to a gatekeeper: who introduces you, and whose word vouches for you
the explicit invitation — permission to record given orally or in writing before any recording begins; without it there is no session
the chain rule — each contact names the next, and a cold approach at the gate fails where a chain succeeds
the reciprocity expectation — access is granted on the understanding that something returns to the community: copies, payment, help, recognition
the outsider's standing — who you are, who sent you, and why you are here are the questions every gatekeeper asks first
the refusal — the documented no, a legitimate outcome and part of the research record
local protocol — the greeting customs, gift norms, and consultation rules that precede any request, as the community defines them
know_how: Map the gatekeepers before arrival: name the people whose permission the community's own musicians need in order to perform, and rank them
Build the introduction chain: get a trusted community member or prior researcher to introduce you, and let each contact open the next door
Ask for permission in person, in the community's language, before recording anything — an explicit invitation, never an implied one
Answer the standing questions — who you are, who sent you, why you are here — plainly, before asking anything of your own
Negotiate the terms of access — what you record, who may hear it, what the community gets back — and document what was agreed
Handle refusal as a result: thank the gatekeeper, document the no, and adjust the study to the access that remains
Follow local protocol for greetings, gifts, and consultation as the community defines it, not as you assume it
habits: Ask 'who must say yes for this to happen?' before every planned recording
Treat the moment the recorder appears as the moment permission must be explicit
Let the chain do the work: every contact names the next, and you follow the names
Record what access you got and how, so the study's evidence base is honest about its limits
Return something before asking for more — reciprocity precedes the next request
nodes.checkpoint: For a real community you intend to study, produce an access plan naming the gatekeepers and the introduction chain to reach them, then secure an explicit invitation — oral or written — to record, and document the terms of access and how a refusal would be handled.
nodes.common_failure: Treating access as logistics: showing up with the recorder and asking anyone 'may I record the music?' — no gatekeeper mapped, no chain, no explicit invitation — so the first session is granted by the wrong person and later denied by the right one, or the recording rests on an assumption that collapses.
sources: Barz & Cooley, Shadows in the Field (2nd ed., 2008), ch. on entry and access
Jeff Todd Titon, 'Knowing Fieldwork' in Shadows in the Field (1997)
SEM position statement on fieldwork ethics
